---
title: "Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment"
subtitle: "Seven on the line, one strong side, five letters and three quarterback depths: the rules and the words that turn eleven players standing still into a readable picture."
description: "The legal-formation rules (seven on the line, who counts as on or off it, covered receivers, illegal formation); formation strength and the three ways to declare it; the receiver alphabet X, Y, Z, H and F with slot, wing, flanker, split end and in-line; quarterback and backfield alignments (under center, shotgun, pistol, offset); receiver splits and the numbers; and how a lineman reports eligible, from the Patriots' January 2015 trick and the 2015 rule to the Lions' eligible tackles."
glossary:
  "On the line / off the line": "Where an offensive player stands at the snap. On the line means level with the center (by rule, the helmet breaks a plane through the center's waist). Off the line means in the backfield, at least a yard behind the line. At least seven players must be on it; a player in between is illegal."
  "Covered receiver": "A player on the line of scrimmage who is not at either end of it, because a teammate is also on the line outside him. On that play he may not catch a forward pass, whatever his position or jersey number."
  "Illegal formation": "A five-yard foul on the offense for lining up wrongly at the snap: fewer than seven players on the line, a player who is neither on the line nor a yard behind it, and similar alignment faults."
  "Formation strength": "The side of a formation treated as its 'strong' side, decided by a rule: usually the tight end's side, sometimes the side with more receivers or the wide side of the field. Offenses name formations by it and defenses set their front and coverage to it."
  "Strong side": "The side of the formation where its strength is: usually the side with the tight end."
  "Weak side": "The side of the formation away from its strength."
  "X receiver": {def: "The wide receiver who lines up on the line of scrimmage, usually alone on the side away from the tight end. He is on the line so that the formation has an end on that side.", aliases: ["Split end"]}
  "Z receiver": {def: "The wide receiver who lines up a yard off the line, usually on the tight end's side, which keeps the tight end eligible and leaves Z free to go in motion.", aliases: ["Flanker"]}
  "Y receiver": "The playbook letter for the main tight end in most NFL offenses. (Some spread systems use Y for a slot receiver.)"
  "H / F (move player)": "Letters for 'move' players whose job changes with the grouping: a slot receiver, a second tight end, an H-back or a fullback. Which letter means what varies from team to team."
  "Slot": "The area between the outside receiver and the end of the offensive line, and the receiver who lines up there, usually off the line."
  "Wing": "A player lined up a yard off the line just outside the end man, usually a tight end or H-back. Being off the line makes him a back: eligible, and free to go in motion."
  "In-line tight end": "A tight end lined up on the line of scrimmage right next to a tackle (attached), where he can block like a lineman or release into a route."
  "Under center": "The quarterback standing directly behind the center with his hands under him, taking the snap hand to hand."
  "Shotgun": "The quarterback standing about five yards behind the center (four to seven, by team) and taking a snap thrown back to him through the air."
  "Pistol": "A hybrid alignment: the quarterback about four yards behind the center and the running back directly behind him, so the back can run straight ahead to either side."
  "Offset back": "A running back or fullback aligned to one side of the quarterback rather than straight behind him. A back beside a shotgun quarterback is often called a 'sidecar'."
  "Split (receiver split)": "How far a receiver lines up from the ball or the formation, usually set by field landmarks such as the numbers and the hash rather than a fixed number of yards."
  "Reduced split": "A receiver lined up closer to the formation than his normal landmark, inside the numbers. A common clue to a block on the inside or a route breaking toward the sideline."
  "The numbers (alignment landmark)": "The painted yard-line numbers, whose tops sit about 14 yards in from each sideline in the NFL. Receivers align by them: 'on the numbers', 'outside the numbers', 'inside the numbers'."
  "Reporting eligible": "How a player wearing a lineman's number (50-79) becomes an eligible receiver for a play: he tells the referee before the snap, the referee announces it so the defense knows, and he lines up at the end of the line or in the backfield."
  "Eligible tackle": {def: "An offensive lineman, usually a tackle, who has reported eligible and lines up at the end of the line, so that he may catch a forward pass on that play.", aliases: ["Tackle-eligible"]}
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared helpers for this chapter's diagrams)"
import logging
import re

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle

from gridiron import Play, Player, defense, style, draw_marker
from gridiron.field import HASH_NEAR, HASH_FAR
from gridiron.formations import LINE_D, TE_W, WING_W, OL_SPLIT

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()

ELIG = style.THIRD          # aqua ring: an eligible receiver
FOUL = "#e34948"            # red ring: the problem (ineligible, or illegal)
TE_RING = style.LINE_TO_GAIN  # gold ring: a tight end (as in Personnel)
OL_RING = "#4a3aa7"         # purple ring: a lineman (as in Personnel)
UC, PIS, GUN, TB_D = -1.9, -4.0, -5.0, -7.0   # QB and back depths, yards behind the line
WIDE, SLOT = 15.0, 9.0      # typical receiver widths from the ball
# Real "off the line" is about a yard deeper than "on the line", less than one marker wide. This chapter's
# formation plates draw off-the-line players deeper (OFF_D) and add a dashed guide, so on/off can be SEEN.
OFF_D = -2.7
GUIDE_D = -1.75             # where the dashed "a yard back" guide is drawn (between the two depths)


def line5():
    """The five offensive linemen; only the center is lettered."""
    return [Player(k, k, "off", LINE_D, w, label=("C" if k == "C" else ""))
            for k, w in [("LT", -2 * OL_SPLIT), ("LG", -OL_SPLIT), ("C", 0.0),
                         ("RG", OL_SPLIT), ("RT", 2 * OL_SPLIT)]]


def P(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    """An offensive skill player at (d, w): d = yards from the line (negative = backfield),
    w = yards to the offense's right of the ball."""
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label or key)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def hide_yard_numbers(ax):
    """Drop the faint painted yard numbers (they sit where receivers stand in these zoomed pictures)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() is not None and abs(t.get_alpha() - 0.55) < 1e-6:
            t.remove()


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=None, ha="center", va="center", fs=7.2, weight="normal", box=True,
        italic=False):
    """A short label at alignment coordinates (d, w), on a light backing so it reads over field lines."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    bb = dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9) if box else None
    return fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=fs, color=color or style.INK, ha=ha, va=va,
                       fontweight=weight, zorder=12, linespacing=1.15, bbox=bb,
                       style="italic" if italic else "normal")


def leader(fld, p, frm, to, color=None, lw=0.6):
    """Thin leader line from a label at frm=(d, w) to a player at to=(d, w)."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(*frm)), fld.xy(*p.to_abs(*to))
    fld.ax.plot([float(x0), float(x1)], [float(y0), float(y1)], color=color or style.INK_2, lw=lw, zorder=6)


def on_line(p):
    return [k for k, q in p.players.items() if q.side == "off" and q.d > -1.0]


def count_line(fld, p, keys, dy=2.9):
    """Number the players on the line, left to right, just in front of each (on a light backing)."""
    for i, k in enumerate(sorted(keys, key=lambda k: p.players[k].w), 1):
        pl = p.players[k]
        x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(pl.d + dy, pl.w))
        fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), str(i), fontsize=6.6, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK,
                    fontweight="bold", zorder=12,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.95))


def depth_guide(fld, p, w0, w1, label_w=None, text="a yard back (depth stretched)"):
    """Dashed guide between 'on the line' and 'a yard off it', from width w0 to w1, with a small label."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(GUIDE_D, w0)), fld.xy(*p.to_abs(GUIDE_D, w1))
    fld.ax.plot([float(x0), float(x1)], [float(y0), float(y1)], color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7,
                ls=(0, (3, 3)), zorder=2.5, alpha=0.8)
    if label_w is not None:
        say(fld, p, GUIDE_D - 0.95, label_w, text, fs=5.8, color=style.INK_2, italic=True, box=False)


def shade_side(fld, p, w0, w1, color, alpha=0.10):
    """Tint the field between widths w0 and w1 (alignment yards) over the whole drawn depth."""
    (xa, _), (xb, _) = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(0, w0)), fld.xy(*p.to_abs(0, w1))
    lo, hi = sorted([float(xa), float(xb)])
    y0, y1 = fld.ax.get_ylim()
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((lo, y0 + 0.5), hi - lo, (y1 - y0) - 1.0, fc=color, ec="none", alpha=alpha,
                               zorder=0.5))


def numbers_band(fld, p, sideline_w, alpha=0.22):
    """Shade the painted-numbers lane, 12 to 14 yards in from the sideline at width sideline_w."""
    s = 1 if sideline_w > 0 else -1
    shade_side(fld, p, sideline_w - s * 12.0, sideline_w - s * 14.0, style.MUTED, alpha=alpha)


def vdim(fld, p, w, d0, d1, text, fs=6.6):
    """A vertical dimension arrow at width w from depth d0 to d1, labelled on its right."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d0, w)), fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d1, w))
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="<|-|>",
                                     mutation_scale=7, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, zorder=6))
    xm, ym = fld.xy(*p.to_abs((d0 + d1) / 2, w + 0.35))
    fld.ax.text(float(xm), float(ym), text, fontsize=fs, color=style.INK, zorder=12, ha="left", va="center")


def hdim(fld, p, d, w0, w1, text, fs=6.3):
    """A horizontal dimension arrow at depth d from width w0 to w1, labelled just below it."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w0)), fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w1))
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="<|-|>",
                                     mutation_scale=7, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, zorder=6))
    say(fld, p, d - 0.75, (w0 + w1) / 2, text, fs=fs)


def referee(fld, p, d, w):
    """The referee: a white, striped disc (officials are neither offense nor defense)."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 0.8, fc="white", ec=style.INK, lw=0.9, hatch="||||", zorder=9))


def pro_11(**moves):
    """11 personnel, under center, 2x2: X on the line left, H in the left slot, Y in-line right,
    Z off the line right, the back 7 yards deep. moves = {key: dict(d=..., w=...)}."""
    off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
                     P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -WIDE), P("H", "WR", OFF_D, -SLOT), P("Z", "WR", OFF_D, WIDE)]
    return [q.moved(**moves[q.key]) if q.key in moves else q for q in off]


def i_form_21():
    """21 personnel, I-formation: X on the line left, Y in-line right, Z off the line right,
    the fullback (F) and the tailback (R) stacked behind the quarterback."""
    return line5() + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("FB", "FB", -4.4, 0, "F"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"),
                      P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -WIDE), P("Z", "WR", OFF_D, WIDE)]
```

First-and-10, ball on the left hash. In the seconds before the snap, three small things happen that the
broadcast barely notices. Out wide on the left, a receiver glances at the official on the sideline, points at
his own chest and gets a nod back. On the right, the tight end settles next to the tackle, and a linebacker
immediately points at him and shouts "Strong right! Strong right!" And the quarterback stops four yards
behind the center, not five, with the running back directly behind him. Each detail answers to something
different: the first to the rulebook, the second to the defense's own language, the third to the offense's
plan. All three are clues. By the end of this chapter you'll know
what the receiver was asking (*am I on the line?*), what the linebacker was shouting about (the formation's
strong side), and why four yards instead of five changes what the offense is likely to do.

**You'll be able to…**

- Check any formation for legality: count seven on the line, find the two ends, spot a covered receiver,
  and say who may catch a forward pass.
- Name a formation's strong side by the tight end, by the receivers and by the field, and say which one a
  defense is likely to use for its front and which for its coverage.
- Label the receivers X, Y, Z, H and F, and use the older names (split end, flanker) and the spot names
  (slot, wing, in-line) the way coaches and broadcasters do.
- Tell under center, shotgun and pistol apart at a glance, and use the quarterback's depth as a run/pass clue
  backed by real numbers.
- Read receiver splits against the numbers and the hash, and say what a reduced split often means.
- Explain how a lineman reports eligible, how the Patriots used the reporting rules against the Ravens in
  January 2015, and what the league changed for the 2015 season.

[Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) told you *who* is on the field. This chapter is about *where*
they stand: the rules every alignment must obey, and the vocabulary coaches use to name it. The next two
chapters use both to build actual formations ([Classic Formations](02-03-classic-formations.qmd) and
[Spread Formations](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)).

## Seven on the line: the rule underneath every formation

You met the core of it in [The Twenty-Two](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd): **at least seven
offensive players on the [line of scrimmage](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)
at the snap**; only the two *ends* of the line and the backs are [eligible
receivers](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) (the quarterback under center excepted); everyone else is
an [ineligible receiver](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd). This chapter asks the questions underneath
that rule. What does "on the line" mean, to the inch? What happens when a formation breaks the rule? And why
would a coach ever want one of his own receivers to be ineligible?

### On the line, off the line, and the gap in between

Every offensive player at the snap is in exactly one of two places, and the rulebook defines both.[^formrules]

- [**On the line**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-on-the-line-off-the-line) means roughly level with the
  center. The rule's test is the helmet: a player is on the line if he faces the defense with his shoulders
  square and his helmet breaks an imaginary vertical wall, parallel to the line, that passes through the
  center's waist. Linemen crouch right up against the ball, so they're obviously on it. A wide receiver thirty
  yards away has to *stand* on it, which is harder to judge.
- **Off the line** means in the backfield, **at least one yard behind the line of scrimmage**. For the offense,
  the line effectively starts at the *back* tip of the ball: the ball's own length, the neutral zone, belongs to
  neither team, and no offensive player may have any part of his body in it. Every back is off the line: the running back,
  the fullback, a receiver standing a yard deep, a tight end set as a wing. The single exception is the
  quarterback under center, who has to be closer than a yard to take the ball from the center's hands.

```{python}
#| label: fig-on-off
#| fig-cap: "On the line, off it, and the illegal strip in between (a close-up of the right half of a formation; depths are stretched so the thin bands show). A player whose helmet reaches the center's waistline is on the line (green band): here the center (C), the guard, the tackle, the tight end (Y) and the receiver (X). A player at least a yard behind the line is a back (blue band), like H. Z is in neither band: too far back to be on the line and too close to be a back, which is an illegal formation. Aqua rings mark eligible receivers; the red ring marks the problem. (Y has no ring: X is on the line outside him, so Y is 'covered', which the next section explains.)"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.1))

ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, y0), x1 - x0, BACK - y0, fc=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.06, ec="none", zorder=1))

ax.add_patch(Ellipse((0, 0.42), 0.34, 0.84, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=9))

    ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", color="white", fontsize=6.5, fontweight="bold", zorder=9)


for x, lab in [(0, "C"), (1.6, ""), (3.2, ""), (4.8, "Y")]:
    man(x, -0.72, lab)
man(12.6, -0.72, "X", ring=ELIG)
man(9.4, -2.0, "Z", ring=FOUL)
man(7.6, -3.75, "H", ring=ELIG)
man(0, -3.1, "Q")
kw = dict(fontsize=7, va="center", ha="left", zorder=10)
ax.text(x1 + 0.3, 0.0, "the offense's line (the\nback tip of the ball)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, **kw)
ax.text(x1 + 0.3, WAIST, "the center's waist", color=style.INK_2, **kw)
ax.text(x1 + 0.3, BACK, "1 yard behind the line", color=style.INK_2, **kw)
ax.text(x1 + 0.3, -3.9, "the backfield", color=style.INK_2, **kw)

        fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
ax.text(8.6, -2.0, "NEITHER ON NOR OFF:\nillegal formation", fontsize=6.6, ha="right", va="center", color=FOUL,
        fontweight="bold", zorder=10)

        color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
ax.text(0.65, -3.1, "QB under center: the\none back allowed closer", fontsize=6.3, ha="left", va="center",
        color=style.INK_2, zorder=10)
```

The strip between those two zones is no-man's land. A player standing half a yard behind the line is neither
on it nor in the backfield, and the formation is illegal. On a crowded line nobody gets stuck there by
accident. But a receiver thirty yards from the ball, looking in at a center he can barely see, can easily end up
half a step off. That's what the receiver in the opening scene was doing: asking the official on his side of
the field, by pointing at himself, whether he was on or off. The wing officials (the line judge and the
down judge, one on each sideline) watch the receivers on their side for exactly this, and receivers
routinely check with them before the snap. The official usually answers with a word or a wave, but he
doesn't have to: he may be busy counting the offense, and the alignment is the receiver's responsibility.[^wing]

Can you see it from your couch? Sometimes. The standard broadcast camera sits high on the sideline, so
compare the receiver's helmet with the helmets of the linemen nearest him: level means on, a visible step
back means off. On a replay from the end-zone camera it's obvious. But you rarely need to judge it by eye,
because the count does the work: find the tight end, and the rule tells you which receiver *has* to be on
the line, as the next sections show.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In *Madden* you can't line up illegally. You pick a formation from a menu, and the game puts every player on
a legal spot. Real formations are built by eleven people walking to marks they memorised, with the play clock
running, a crowd screaming and a receiver who can't hear the quarterback. Every snap, the officials check the
count and the depths, and the defense checks them too, because the alignment tells it who can catch the
ball. A one-yard mistake is a flag, and a one-yard *choice* is a clue.
:::

Why seven? The rule is older than the forward pass as we know it. In the early 1900s, college football's
signature plays were "mass" plays: wedges and pile-drives in which most of the offense lined up behind the
ball and crashed into one spot with a running start. Players were being badly hurt and killed, and in 1905 the
sport came close to being banned. The rule makers spent the next few years reshaping the game, and by 1910
they required seven men on the line of scrimmage, so that most of the offense had to start from a standstill
on the line instead of building momentum behind it.[^seven] The seven-man line was a safety rule. Its
modern job is different: it guarantees that the offense always has five big, ineligible blockers in the
middle, and it forces the offense to *declare* its receivers by where they stand.

None of this binds the defense. On a scrimmage play it may line up anyone anywhere on its own side of the
neutral zone, in any number, and move around before the snap; its only alignment rule is to stay out of the
neutral zone.[^defalign] That asymmetry runs through the whole book: the offense has to show its hand by
rule, and the defense gets to disguise.

### Illegal formation

When an alignment breaks those rules, the officials throw a flag for [**illegal
formation**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-illegal-formation): a five-yard penalty on the offense for
lining up wrongly at the snap. The common versions are the ones in the next picture: fewer than seven players
on the line, or a player stuck in no-man's land.

```{python}
#| label: fig-legal-illegal
#| fig-cap: "Three versions of the same 11-personnel formation (X, H, Z = wide receivers, Y = tight end, R = running back, Q = quarterback under center; the linemen are unlettered apart from the center, C). Players behind the dashed line are a yard off the line (depths stretched so you can see it). The small numbers count the players on the line; aqua rings mark the eligible receivers, red rings the problem. 1: legal. 2: X has stepped back a yard: six on the line, illegal formation. 3: Z has stepped up instead: eight on the line is legal, but Y is now covered."
titles = {"legal": "1.  Legal: seven on the line",
          "six": "2.  Illegal formation: only six on the line",
          "covered": "3.  Legal, but the tight end is covered"}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.6, 7.4))
for ax, case in zip(axes, ["legal", "six", "covered"]):
    moves = {"six": {"X": dict(d=OFF_D)}, "covered": {"Z": dict(d=LINE_D)}}.get(case, {})
    p = Play(pro_11(**moves), None, los=40, to_go=None)
    for k in {"legal": ["X", "H", "Y", "Z", "RB"], "six": [], "covered": ["X", "H", "Z", "RB"]}[case]:
        p.highlight(k, color=ELIG)
    if case == "six":
        p.highlight("X", color=FOUL)
    if case == "covered":
        p.highlight("Y", color=FOUL)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-9.4, 4.4), title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    depth_guide(fld, p, -19.0, 19.0, label_w=9.4)
    count_line(fld, p, on_line(p))
    ax.set_title(titles[case], loc="left", fontsize=9, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    if case == "legal":
        say(fld, p, -5.0, -15.0, "X: the left end, eligible", fs=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -5.2, 15.0, "Y is the right end; Z,\na yard back, is a back", fs=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -5.6, 2.2, "Q under center:\nnot eligible", fs=6.6, ha="left")
    if case == "six":
        say(fld, p, -5.4, -15.0, "X stepped back:\nnow he's a back too", fs=6.8, color=FOUL)
        say(fld, p, -5.4, 13.0, "five men in the backfield:\nillegal formation, 5 yards", fs=6.8)
    if case == "covered":
        say(fld, p, -5.2, 15.0, "Z stepped up: now he\nis the right end", fs=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -5.4, 8.2, "Y: on the line but not\nat the end, so ineligible", fs=6.8, color=FOUL)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

Notice what panel 3 says about the word "illegal." Covering your own tight end is **not** an illegal formation.
Eight on the line is fine; the rule says *at least* seven. The formation is legal, but the tight end can't catch a
forward pass on that play. If the ball is thrown to him anyway, that's a different foul, an ineligible player
touching a pass, and the penalties are in [Contact Rules and
Penalties](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd).

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"An unusual-looking formation must be illegal."** Almost never. Eight men on the line is legal. Two
receivers stacked one behind the other is legal. Two tackles side by side on one side of the center is
legal (that's an [unbalanced line](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd), the subject of
[Spread Formations](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)). A lineman standing at the end of the line and
catching a pass is legal, if he reported (below). The legality test is short: **seven or more on the line,
nobody in no-man's land, no more than one man moving at the snap** (the motion rules from [The Pre-Snap
Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)), and the right people eligible. Weird is allowed. That's
why offenses get away with so much.
:::

## Covered receivers, and why X stands on the line

A [**covered receiver**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-covered-receiver) is a player who is on the line of
scrimmage but not at either end of it, because a teammate is also on the line outside him. He's ineligible on
that play, whatever his jersey number and whatever his position. In panel 3 above, the tight end was covered
by the Z receiver.

Here's the elegant part. The covered-receiver rule explains the most basic habit in receiver alignment, one
you saw in [The Twenty-Two](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) without a reason: **the X receiver
lines up on the line, and the Z receiver lines up a yard off it.**

Look again at panel 1. The formation has a tight end attached to the right side of the line. If the receiver
on that side also stood on the line, he would cover the tight end, and the offense's most versatile player
would be a blocker only. So the receiver on the tight end's side (Z) stands a yard back. That keeps Y as the
right end and eligible, and as a bonus it makes Z a back, which means Z is the one who can go in
[motion](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) (only an off-the-line player may move at the snap).
On the other side there's no tight end, so *somebody* has to be the left end, and someone has to be the
seventh man on the line. That's X's job: he stands on the line so the formation has seven and an end on that
side. The letters didn't come first. The rule did, and the letters name the jobs it creates.

The same logic places the slot receiver (H in panel 1). If H stood on the line inside X, X would cover him. So
the general rule is: **on each side, only the outermost man on the line can catch a pass, and anyone inside
him who wants to run a route has to stand a yard back.** That's why slot receivers, wings and backs are all
"off the ball".

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: covering on purpose"}
Why would an offense *choose* to cover one of its own eligible receivers, as in panel 3? Three common reasons.

- **To free someone else to move.** Only a back may be in motion at the snap. Putting one receiver on the
  line (and covering the tight end) can let a different receiver line up a yard back and go in motion.
- **To build a formation the defense hasn't seen.** A tight end who is covered is a sixth blocker. On a
  pass play he may not go more than a yard past the line before the ball is thrown (that would be an
  ineligible man downfield, the same rule that holds every lineman back).[^downfield] So he can't really run a
  route, and if the defense doesn't notice, it wastes a defender covering him.
- **To change who the defense must account for.** Every eligible receiver needs a defender. Making one
  ineligible, and making another eligible, changes the count.

The cost is the obvious one: a covered player can't catch the ball, and an alert defense that spots it can
treat him as a blocker. Covering is a deliberate trade of one threat for another.
:::

## Formation strength: which side is "strong"?

The linebacker in the opening scene was shouting about the **formation's strength**. Every formation has two
sides, and teams need a shared word for which side is which, because almost everything else (who lines up
where, which way the run goes, how the coverage tilts) is described relative to it.

[**Formation strength**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-formation-strength) is the side of a formation
treated as its "strong" side, decided by a rule. The side it names is the [**strong
side**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-strong-side); the other is the [**weak
side**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-weak-side). Offenses use strength to name formations ("Trips Right"
means three receivers to the right, and most formation names carry a "Right" or "Left" like it), and defenses call it out loud
before every snap, so all eleven defenders set to the same side. What makes this interesting is that there is
more than one rule for deciding it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-strength
#| fig-cap: "Three ways to declare strength (all three panels at the same scale). 1: by the tight end. The offense is 21 personnel in an I-formation (a fullback, F, in front of the tailback, R) with its tight end (gold ring) attached on the right, so the right is the strong side, and a 4-3 defense sets to it: the strong-side linebacker (S, the Sam) lines up over the tight end and the strong safety (SS) moves down toward that side (E = end, T = tackle, M and W = the other linebackers, CB = cornerback, FS = free safety). 2: two strengths at once. The tight end is alone on the left, but three receivers are on the right; many defenses set the front to the tight end and lean the coverage toward the three receivers. 3: by the field. In a balanced 2x2 with no attached tight end (Y is flexed out in the slot), the ball is on the left hash, so the right side has about six more yards of room; many defenses then call the strength to the wide side."
H_ = 53.33
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.6, 8.6),
                         gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[24.0 / H_, 13.6 / H_, 13.6 / H_]))
# 1. tight-end strength: 21 personnel, I-formation, against a 4-3 'over' front set to it
off = i_form_21()
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off)
fix = {"LCB": dict(d=6.5, w=-WIDE), "RCB": dict(d=6.5, w=WIDE), "SS": dict(d=8.5, w=7.5),
       "FS": dict(d=13.0, w=-1.0), "SAM": dict(d=3.5, w=6.8), "WILL": dict(d=4.5, w=-3.4),
       "MIKE": dict(d=4.5, w=0.9)}
dfn = [q.moved(**fix[q.key]) if q.key in fix else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(label="CB") if q.pos == "CB" else q for q in dfn]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None)
p.highlight("Y", color=TE_RING)
p.highlight("SAM", "SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
ax = axes[0]
fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral="full", window=(-8.6, 15.4), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(ax)
shade_side(fld, p, 0.4, 26.6, style.OFFENSE)
ax.set_title("1.  Tight-end strength: the run game's definition", loc="left", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold",
             color=style.INK)
say(fld, p, 13.0, 15.5, "STRONG SIDE\n(the tight end's side)", fs=7, weight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(fld, p, 13.0, -15.5, "WEAK SIDE", fs=7, weight="bold", color=style.INK_2)
say(fld, p, 9.9, 16.5, "S and SS line up\nto the strength", fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, -4.4, -4.6, "F: fullback", fs=6.4)
# 2. tight-end strength one way, passing strength the other
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, -TE_W),
                 P("X", "WR", LINE_D, 16.5), P("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 11.5), P("H", "WR", OFF_D, 7.2)]
p = Play(off, None, los=40, to_go=None)
p.highlight("Y", color=TE_RING)
ax = axes[1]
fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral="full", window=(-8.6, 5.0), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(ax)
shade_side(fld, p, -26.6, -0.4, style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.07)
shade_side(fld, p, 0.4, 26.6, style.THIRD, alpha=0.10)
ax.set_title("2.  Two strengths at once: tight end one way, receivers the other", loc="left", fontsize=9,
             fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
say(fld, p, 2.7, -13.5, "TE STRENGTH\n(the front usually sets here)", fs=7, weight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(fld, p, 2.7, 12.5, "PASSING STRENGTH: three receivers\n(the coverage usually leans here)", fs=7,
    weight="bold", color="#127a55")
# 3. field strength: balanced 2x2, ball on the left hash
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -WIDE),
                 P("H", "WR", OFF_D, -SLOT), P("Y", "TE", OFF_D, SLOT), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, WIDE)]
p = Play(off, None, los=40, ball_y="left", to_go=None)
p.highlight("Y", color=TE_RING)
ax = axes[2]
fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral="full", window=(-8.6, 5.0), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(ax)
shade_side(fld, p, 0.4, HASH_FAR, style.LINE_TO_GAIN, alpha=0.12)
ax.set_title("3.  Field strength: balanced, so call it to the wide side", loc="left", fontsize=9,
             fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
say(fld, p, 2.7, 15.0, "FIELD SIDE: 29.75 yards of room", fs=7, weight="bold", color="#9a6a00")
say(fld, p, 2.7, -12.0, "BOUNDARY: 23.6 yards", fs=7, weight="bold", color=style.INK_2)
say(fld, p, -6.6, 2.0, "ball on the left hash", fs=6.6, ha="left")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

**Tight-end strength (panel 1)** is the oldest rule and the one most fronts still use. The strong side is the
side with the [tight end](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd), or, with two tight ends, the side with
more of them (or with the tight end plus a wing). Why the tight end? Because he is a blocker standing on the
line. An attached tight end adds a blocker *and* adds one more running lane to defend: there's now a gap
outside him that didn't exist before (gaps are named and numbered in [Run Game
Language](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd)). More blockers and more gaps on one side means
the run game is stronger there, so the defense puts more of its run defenders there. That's why two defensive
positions are *named* for it: the [Sam linebacker](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) ("strong-side
linebacker") and the [strong safety](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) both line up toward the tight
end, as in panel 1. The logic only works while the tight end is *attached*, standing next to the tackle. Flex
him out into the slot, as in panel 3, and he no longer adds a gap or a blocker at the line, so most defenses
stop counting him for the front and treat him like any other receiver.

**Passing strength (panel 2)** counts receivers. The side with more eligible receivers lined up away from the
ball, usually the side with three in a 3x1 set (a formation with three receivers on one side and one on the
other, built properly in [Spread Formations](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)), is the passing
strength. Coverage cares about this side, because that's where the defenders who cover receivers are needed.
Coaches number those receivers from the outside in: the outermost is #1, the next #2, the next #3. The count
includes the tight end, and it includes a back once he lines up or releases to that side: he becomes the next
number in the count, #3 beside two receivers or #4 beside three. A back directly behind the quarterback isn't
counted until he picks a side. You'll see the numbers in the label map below, and they come
back in every coverage chapter.

**Field strength (panel 3)** ignores the offense entirely. When the ball is on a [hash
mark](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd), one side of the field (the [field
side](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd)) has about six more yards of room than the other
(the [boundary side](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd)). Room is where offenses like to
attack, especially on the edges, so some defenses simply declare the field the strong side every snap. It's
common in college, where the hashes are much wider and the difference between the two sides is about
thirteen yards rather than six, and it's the natural tiebreaker in the NFL when the offense is balanced.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: one word, eleven players"}
Strength exists so that **eleven defenders can line up correctly in two seconds without discussing it**. The
defense's call names the front and the coverage *relative to* the strength (an "over" front shifts the
defensive line toward the strength, an "under" front away from it, both built in [Even
Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-02-even-fronts.qmd); "rotate to strength" sends a safety
toward it), so the same call works whichever way the offense lines up. The linebacker shouting "Strong right!"
is translating the call for this snap.

The offense knows that, so it plays with the definition. It can put the tight end on one side and the
receivers on the other (panel 2), forcing the defense to pick which rule wins. It can line up balanced, so the
defense has to fall back on the field. And it can [shift](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) its
tight end across at the last moment, so that the strength the defense declared is suddenly the weak side,
which is exactly the shift you watched in [The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd).
Every one of those moves costs the offense something (time, a simpler play, a predictable look), and it buys a
defense that is late or wrong.
:::

Which rule do NFL defenses use? It varies by team and by call, and good defenses use more than one. A
common pattern is the one in panel 2: **the front sets to the tight end, the coverage to the passing
strength**, with the field as the tiebreaker when the formation is balanced and has no attached tight end.

Real defenses don't say "strong right," which is the textbook version. They use code words, and because the
front and the coverage can set to different sides, many staffs keep separate words for each. Nick Saban's
defenses made "Rip" and "Liz" (right and left) famous as the call for the passing strength, and other staffs
use "Roscoe" and "Louie" or a number; a call such as "Rita Sky!" can carry the strength and the coverage in
two words.[^strengthcalls] The exact words vary by staff, but the idea doesn't: one word, both strengths, before
every snap. Offenses have the matching dialect problem. In many pro-style playbooks the "Right" in a
formation's name tells the tight end where to line up; in many spread playbooks it names the side of the
three receivers ([Offensive Systems and
Languages](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd) compares them).

You don't need to know a defense's rulebook to use any of this. You only need to name the candidates before
the snap and then see which one the defense chose. That is the drill in "Watch for it on Sunday" below.

## The receiver alphabet: X, Y, Z, H and F

Listen to a coach or an analyst for long enough and you'll hear letters: "the X ran a slant," "they put the Y in
the slot," "F motion." The letters name **spots in the formation**, not people, so that one play call can tell
every player his job regardless of who is filling the spot that day. "X runs a slant" works whether the X is a
star or his backup.

```{python}
#| label: fig-label-map
#| fig-cap: "The receiver alphabet on three common formations (aqua rings = eligible receivers; players behind the dashed line are a yard off the line, depth stretched). Top, 11 personnel in a 2x2 under center: X, the split end, on the line away from the tight end; H in the slot on that side; Y, the in-line tight end; Z, the flanker, a yard off the line outside him. Middle, 11 personnel in a 3x1 from the shotgun: X alone on the weak side and three receivers to the right, numbered from the outside in. (A shotgun quarterback is technically eligible too; see the quarterback section.) Bottom, 21 personnel in an I-formation: F is the fullback."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.6, 8.1))
WIN = (-9.4, 3.6)
p = Play(pro_11(), None, los=40, to_go=None)
p.highlight("X", "Y", "Z", "H", "RB", color=ELIG)
fld = p.draw(ax=axes[0], lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=WIN, title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(axes[0])
depth_guide(fld, p, -19.0, 19.0)
axes[0].set_title("2x2: two receivers on each side (11 personnel, under center)", loc="left", fontsize=9,
                  fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
say(fld, p, -3.6, -WIDE, "X  split end\non the line", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -5.2, -SLOT, "H  slot\noff the line", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -3.7, TE_W + 0.9, "Y  in-line\ntight end", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -5.2, WIDE, "Z  flanker\noff the line", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -7.2, 1.6, "R  the back", fs=6.8, ha="left")
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
                 P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -WIDE), P("H", "WR", OFF_D, 10.2), P("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 16.2)]
p = Play(off, None, los=40, to_go=None)
p.highlight("X", "Y", "Z", "H", "RB", color=ELIG)
fld = p.draw(ax=axes[1], lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=WIN, title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(axes[1])
depth_guide(fld, p, -19.0, 19.0)
axes[1].set_title("3x1: three on one side, one on the other (11 personnel, shotgun)", loc="left", fontsize=9,
                  fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
say(fld, p, -3.6, -WIDE, "X  alone on the\nweak side", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -3.7, TE_W + 0.6, "Y  in-line\n(#3)", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -5.2, 10.2, "H  slot\n(#2)", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -5.2, 16.4, "Z  flanker\n(#1)", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -7.4, -2.2, "R  beside the Q", fs=6.8)
p = Play(i_form_21(), None, los=40, to_go=None)
p.highlight("X", "Y", "Z", "FB", "RB", color=ELIG)
fld = p.draw(ax=axes[2], lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=WIN, title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(axes[2])
depth_guide(fld, p, -19.0, 19.0)
axes[2].set_title("I-formation: two backs (21 personnel, under center)", loc="left", fontsize=9,
                  fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
say(fld, p, -3.6, -WIDE, "X  split end\non the line", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -3.7, TE_W + 0.9, "Y  in-line\ntight end", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -5.2, WIDE, "Z  flanker\noff the line", fs=6.8)
say(fld, p, -4.4, 1.6, "F  the fullback", fs=6.8, ha="left")
say(fld, p, -7.2, 1.6, "R  the tailback", fs=6.8, ha="left")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2)
plt.show()
```

Here is the alphabet as most NFL playbooks use it. Teams differ, and the differences are noted.

- The [**X receiver**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-x-receiver), or [**split
  end**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-split-end), lines up **on the line**, usually alone on the side away
  from the tight end. He is the end of the line on that side, which is why the older name calls him an "end"
  who has "split" away from the tackle. Being on the line has a cost: he can't go in motion, and a cornerback
  can line up right in his face and jam him at the snap (playing
  [press](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-press), as [The Twenty-Two](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd)
  called it). So the X is often a big, strong receiver who can beat that contact, frequently the team's best.
- The [**Z receiver**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-z-receiver), or
  [**flanker**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flanker), lines up **a yard off the line**, usually on the
  tight end's side. Being off the ball keeps the tight end uncovered, gives Z a little more room against a
  jam, and makes him the receiver most often sent in motion.
- The [**Y receiver**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-y-receiver) is, in most NFL offenses, the main tight
  end. (Some spread systems use Y for a slot receiver instead, among them the Air Raid, a pass-first college
  system covered in [Offensive Systems and Languages](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd).)
- **H** and **F** are the [**move players**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-h-f-move-player), letters for
  whoever fills the flexible spots in a given grouping. In 11 personnel, H is usually the third receiver, in
  the slot. In 12 personnel, H may be a second tight end. In 21 personnel, F is often the
  [fullback](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) (bottom panel). Some teams swap the two letters, and
  in some systems F is the slot and H the back. When a broadcaster says "the F," check what body type is
  standing there.
- Two more letters fill out the diagrams in this book. Many NFL playbooks call the second tight end **U**
  (others use H or F for him), and the running back gets a letter of his own, usually **R**, **T** or **B**
  depending on the system. This book uses U and R.

The older names come from the era when receivers were converted backs and ends. A "flanker" was originally a
halfback flanked out wide of the formation, an innovation of the Los Angeles Rams around 1949–50, who
moved halfback Elroy "Crazylegs" Hirsch out wide to catch passes and turned him into one of the great
receivers of the decade.[^flanker] The "split end" was an end who split away from his tackle. The words stuck
even after the jobs became full-time receiver positions.

The spot names complete the vocabulary:

- The [**slot**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slot) is the area between the outside receiver and the end of
  the line, and the **slot receiver** is the one who lines up there, off the line (for the reason you saw above:
  on the line, he'd be covered). The slot is the best place on the field to get open quickly: the receiver can
  break inside or outside (a "two-way go"), is hard to jam, and is usually covered by a linebacker, a safety or
  the [slot cornerback](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) rather than a team's best cover man.
- An [**in-line tight end**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-in-line-tight-end) is attached to the line,
  right next to a tackle, where he is both a sixth blocker and an eligible end.
- An **H-back** is a tight end (or a fullback-sized player) who lines up in the backfield, just off the
  tackle's outside hip, instead of on the line. From there he can lead the runner through a hole (block for
  him, a step ahead of him), kick out an edge defender, or slip into a route. Joe Gibbs made the position
  famous in Washington in the 1980s; [Run Game Language](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) tells
  that story.
- A [**wing**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wing) is a player lined up a yard off the line just outside
  the end man, usually a tight end or an H-back. A wing is a back: eligible, free to go in motion, and well
  placed to block an edge defender or slip into a route.

A tight end isn't stuck in one spot. Here are the places he can stand, each with its own name and its own
message to the defense:

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-spots
#| fig-cap: "One tight end (gold ring), five places he can stand, one at a time (each marker is a different snap; depth stretched, as before). On the left, a wing: a yard off the line, within a yard or so of the tackle's outside shoulder. On the right, from the ball outward: in-line (attached), a blocker first but eligible; H-back (offset), in the backfield off the tackle's hip, ready to lead, kick out or release; flexed (detached), off the line a few yards outside, now mostly a receiver; split wide, where a receiver would stand, often hunting a mismatch against a smaller defender."
spots = [(OFF_D, -4.6, "WING\na yard off the line,\njust outside the tackle", (-6.0, -8.0)),
         (LINE_D, TE_W, "IN-LINE (attached)\non the line, next\nto the tackle", (2.9, 2.4)),
         (-4.4, 4.2, "H-BACK (offset)\nin the backfield,\noff the tackle's hip", (-7.3, 4.2)),
         (OFF_D, 10.0, "FLEXED (detached)\noff the line, a few\nyards outside", (2.9, 10.6)),
         (LINE_D, 17.5, "SPLIT WIDE\nwhere a receiver\nwould stand", (-5.6, 17.3))]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
p = Play(line5() + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q")], None, los=40, to_go=None)
fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-14.5, 23.0), window=(-9.4, 5.4), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(ax)
depth_guide(fld, p, -13.0, 20.5)
ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
for d, w, txt, at in spots:
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    draw_marker(ax, float(x), float(y), "off", "Y", ppy, ring=TE_RING)
    leader(fld, p, at, (d, w))
    say(fld, p, at[0], at[1], txt, fs=6.4)
plt.show()
```

The farther a tight end stands from the tackle, the more he says "receiver" and the less he says "blocker."
That's the same personnel-versus-formation gap you met in [Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd): the
defense matched a tight end's *body*, and now the offense chooses how much of a receiver to make him. (And, as
you saw under strength, once he detaches from the tackle most defenses stop setting the front to him.)

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"The X is the number-one receiver."** Often he is, because the spot suits a big, complete receiver, but the
letter names the spot, not the star. Plenty of teams move their best receiver around precisely so the defense
can't find him by looking for the X. A star receiver might be the X on one snap, the Z on the
next and in the slot on the third. Use the letters to read the formation, and use the roster to read
the matchup.
:::

## Where the quarterback stands: under center, pistol, shotgun

The quarterback's depth is the easiest alignment clue to see on a broadcast, because the camera is behind the
offense and the quarterback is in the middle of the picture. There are three basic depths, and each one exists
because it solves a different problem. (Two rarer looks complete the set: an *empty* backfield, with the
running back split out as a receiver, and a direct snap to a running back with the quarterback split wide, the
*Wildcat*. Both belong to [Spread Formations](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd).)

```{python}
#| label: fig-qb-depths
#| fig-cap: "The three quarterback depths, with typical distances (they vary by team and quarterback). Under center: the quarterback (Q) takes the ball from the center's hands; the back (R) is about seven yards deep, straight behind him. (Q is drawn a little deeper than real life so the markers don't overlap.) Pistol: the quarterback about four yards back, the back right behind him. Shotgun: the quarterback about five yards back, and the back usually beside him, offset to one side."
cases = [("Under center", UC, (TB_D, 0.0), None,
          "hands under the center;\nthe back about 7 yards\ndeep, straight behind"),
         ("Pistol", PIS, (TB_D, 0.0), "~4 yd",
          "quarterback about 4 yards\ndeep, the back 2-3 yards\nstraight behind him"),
         ("Shotgun", GUN, (GUN, 2.2), "~5 yd",
          "quarterback about 5 yards\ndeep (4-7 by team), the\nback beside him: 'offset'")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
for ax, (name, qd, (rd, rw), qtxt, desc) in zip(axes, cases):
    p = Play(line5() + [P("QB", "QB", qd, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", rd, rw, "R")], None, los=40, to_go=None)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-7.6, 7.6), window=(-9.6, 2.0), title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    ax.set_title(name, loc="center", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    if qtxt is None:
        leader(fld, p, (-3.4, -3.6), (-1.9, -0.6))
        say(fld, p, -3.9, -3.6, "QB's hands\nunder the C", fs=6.4)
    else:
        vdim(fld, p, -5.2, 0.0, qd, qtxt)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.03, desc, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK,
            linespacing=1.2)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
fig.subplots_adjust(bottom=0.2)
plt.show()
```

### Under center

[**Under center**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-under-center) means the quarterback stands directly behind
the center with his hands under him and takes the snap hand to hand. It was the only way to play quarterback
for most of the NFL's history, and it is still the best way to do two things.

**Run downhill.** The back starts about seven yards deep, directly behind the quarterback, and takes the
handoff already moving forward at speed, with the whole line in front of him and the choice of going left or
right still open. **Fake the run.** On [play-action](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)
(faking a handoff, then throwing), an under-center quarterback turns his back to the defense to make the fake,
and the linebackers see exactly what a real run looks like. That's the whole point of the fake.

What it gives up: to pass, the quarterback has to drop back three, five or seven steps while the rush comes,
and during the first steps of that drop he isn't looking at the defense at all. From under center he also
can't see much over 300-pound linemen until he gets depth.

### Shotgun

In the [**shotgun**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shotgun), the quarterback stands about five yards behind
the center (four to seven, depending on the team and the quarterback) and the center throws the ball back to
him through the air. Now the quarterback is already at passing depth when he catches the snap. He sees the
whole defense the instant the ball arrives, he can throw quickly without a drop, and he has an extra beat
against the pass rush. Those advantages are why the shotgun became the NFL's default as the league passed more:
in the nflverse play-by-play it was on about one run or pass in five in 2006 and about two in three in the
2020s, a story told with the data in [Classic Formations](02-03-classic-formations.qmd).

The shotgun is older than it looks. The San Francisco 49ers under coach Red Hickey introduced it in 1960, with
the quarterback set deep to buy time against a fierce pass rush, and it beat the Colts with it before defenses
caught up and the formation faded. Tom Landry's Dallas Cowboys revived it in 1975 as a passing-down weapon
for Roger Staubach, and from there it spread.[^shotgun]

What the shotgun gives up is mostly in the run game. The back usually lines up *beside* the quarterback, not
behind him, so he starts moving sideways and takes the handoff going across the formation rather than
straight ahead. The snap travels five yards through the air, so it can be fumbled. And the play-action fake is
less convincing, because the quarterback never turns his back.

The shotgun has one rules quirk worth knowing. The under-center exception you met at the start of the chapter
covers only a quarterback within a yard of the center. A shotgun quarterback is five yards deep, so he is a
back like any other, and an **eligible receiver**.[^qbelig] That's what makes trick plays to the quarterback
legal. The most famous is the "Philly Special" in Super Bowl LII (February 2018, the 2017 season): Nick Foles
walked up behind the right tackle as if to change the play, the ball was snapped directly to running back Corey
Clement, tight end Trey Burton took a pitch from him and threw, and Foles, by rule a back, caught the
touchdown on fourth-and-goal.[^phillyspecial]

### Pistol

The [**pistol**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pistol) is the compromise. The quarterback stands about four
yards back, a short shotgun, and the running back lines up directly behind *him*, two or three yards deeper.
Nevada coach Chris Ault designed it in 2005, looking for a way to keep the shotgun's view of the defense and
still give his back a straight, downhill run to either side.[^pistol] Ault's Nevada quarterback Colin
Kaepernick took it to the NFL, and by 2012 the 49ers and Washington were running pistol option plays at the
pro level ([Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) tells that story).

The pistol's quiet advantage is that it **hides the direction of the run**. A back offset to one side of a
shotgun quarterback tells the defense something about where the handoff can go; a back straight behind the
quarterback tells it nothing. That is the answer to the opening scene's third question: a quarterback at four
yards with the back behind him is in the alignment built for running downhill, and, as the numbers below show,
NFL teams use it that way.

### Offset backs and the sidecar

An [**offset back**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-offset-back) is a running back or fullback aligned to one
side of the quarterback rather than directly behind him. Under center, a fullback offset a step to one side
of the tailback (an "offset I," named in [Classic Formations](02-03-classic-formations.qmd)) leans the play
toward that side. In the shotgun, the back nearly always stands to one side, often right beside the
quarterback, a spot coaches call the **sidecar**. Where he stands is a clue, never a guarantee: on many
shotgun runs the handoff goes *away* from the back's side, with the back crossing in front of the quarterback,
and in pass protection he may block his own side or cross the quarterback's face, depending on the
protection call ([Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd)). Different teams run different rules, which is why
your [prediction log](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) should track the back's side for
the team you watch.

### What the depth tells you

So much for the reasons. Here is what offenses actually do from each depth. The data is **charting**: people
at a company called FTN watch every NFL play on film and tag what they see, including where the quarterback
lined up, and nflverse publishes their tags for free. Three seasons of it:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (load FTN charting: quarterback alignment, 2023-2025)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

QB_SEASONS = [2023, 2024, 2025]
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting(QB_SEASONS).to_pandas()
cols = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "play_type", "down", "ydstogo", "pass", "wp",
        "half_seconds_remaining"]
plays = pbp(QB_SEASONS, columns=cols)
plays = plays[(plays.season_type == "REG") & plays.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & plays.down.notna()]
qb = plays.merge(ftn[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "qb_location", "is_play_action"]],
                 left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"])
qb["qb_location"] = qb.qb_location.astype(str).str.strip()     # U = under center, P = pistol, S = shotgun
qb = qb[qb.qb_location.isin(["U", "P", "S"])]
# neutral: 1st and 2nd down, win probability 20-80%, outside the last two minutes of each half
neutral = qb[qb.down.isin([1, 2]) & qb.wp.between(0.2, 0.8) & (qb.half_seconds_remaining > 120)]
ORDER = ["U", "P", "S"]
NAMES = {"U": "Under center", "P": "Pistol", "S": "Shotgun"}
qb_share = neutral.qb_location.value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(ORDER) * 100
qb_pass = neutral.groupby("qb_location")["pass"].mean().reindex(ORDER) * 100
qb_pa = neutral[neutral["pass"] == 1].groupby("qb_location").is_play_action.mean().reindex(ORDER) * 100
long3 = qb[(qb.down == 3) & (qb.ydstogo >= 7)].qb_location.value_counts(normalize=True) * 100
short34 = qb[qb.down.isin([3, 4]) & (qb.ydstogo <= 1)].qb_location.value_counts(normalize=True) * 100
# who lives in the pistol: each team-season's pistol share of its runs and passes (all situations)
pistol_ts = (qb.assign(pis=qb.qb_location.eq("P")).groupby(["season", "posteam"]).pis.mean() * 100
             ).sort_values(ascending=False)
pistol_all = qb.qb_location.eq("P").mean() * 100
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-qb-tells
#| fig-cap: "What the quarterback's depth tells you. Under center and pistol lean run; the shotgun leans pass; and when an under-center quarterback does drop back to pass, it is almost always after a run fake. Neutral situations (1st and 2nd down, win probability 20–80%, outside the last two minutes of each half), 2023–2025 regular seasons, FTN charting via nflverse. Left, the share of plays that were dropbacks (passes, sacks and scrambles). Right, of those dropbacks, the share with a play-action fake. The labels give each alignment's share of these neutral plays, which is why the shotgun's share is lower here than across all plays."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.5), sharey=True)
colors = [style.OFFENSE_DARK, style.MUTED, style.OFFENSE]
for ax, vals, title in [(axes[0], qb_pass, "Pass rate"), (axes[1], qb_pa, "Play-action share of dropbacks")]:
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.barh(range(3), vals.values, color=colors, height=0.62)
    for i, v in enumerate(vals.values):
        ax.text(v + 1.5, i, f"{v:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9.5)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.set_xticks([0, 25, 50, 75, 100], ["0", "25", "50", "75", "100%"], fontsize=7.5)
axes[0].set_yticks(range(3), [f"{NAMES[k]}\n({qb_share[k]:.0f}% of plays)" for k in ORDER], fontsize=8)
axes[0].invert_yaxis()
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.5)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
assert 60 < qb_pass["S"] < 78 and 25 < qb_pass["U"] < 42 and qb_pa["U"] > 70, (qb_pass, qb_pa)
assert long3["S"] > 95 and short34["U"] > 55, (long3, short34)
assert pistol_ts.index[0][1] == "ATL" and pistol_ts.iloc[0] > 30 and 4 < pistol_all < 9, (pistol_ts.head(), pistol_all)
assert 45 < qb_share["S"] < 60 and 33 < qb_share["U"] < 45, qb_share
```

This is one of the strongest single clues in the course, much stronger than personnel alone. In neutral
situations from 2023 to 2025, offenses threw on about **69% of shotgun plays** but only about **34% of
under-center plays** and **28% of pistol plays**.[^qbdata] And when they *did* throw from under center, it was
almost always a fake: about **81% of under-center dropbacks used play-action**, against about 21% from the
shotgun. Under center has become, in effect, the run-and-play-action alignment.

A note on the shares in the chart's labels, because they differ from the ones earlier in the section. Across
*all* plays the shotgun is on about two in three. On the early downs of close games, which is where the
formation choice tells you the most, offenses go under center far more often, and the shotgun drops to about
half. Same data, different slice.

The pistol is the surprise: it's even more run-heavy than under center. That's the opening scene's answer.
NFL teams use the pistol as a *running* alignment that keeps the quarterback off the center: the back gets
his straight, downhill start, and the quarterback can still read the defense or keep the ball on an option.
It's also a niche look, about 6% of all plays, concentrated in a few offenses. Atlanta lined up in it on about
a third of its plays in both 2024 and 2025, and Miami on nearly 30% in 2024. (It isn't mainly a Ravens look:
Baltimore was at about 7%, ninth in the league.)[^pistolteams]

The situational extremes are starker still. On third-and-7 or longer, offenses were in the shotgun on about
97% of plays. On third- or fourth-and-1, they were under center about 61% of the time, because a quarterback
who takes the snap hand to hand can sneak (simply lunge forward behind the center), hand off going forward,
or fake it all in one motion.

None of this makes the shotgun a pass signal you can bet the house on. Thirty percent of neutral shotgun plays
were runs, and the best offenses work hard to keep their tendencies honest. But the under-center share has been
climbing: in the charting data it rose to about a third of all plays in 2025, up from about 27% in 2023.[^uctrend]
As offenses went back under center, the quarterback's depth became a more useful clue, not a less useful one.

## Splits and landmarks: how wide is wide?

A receiver's [**split**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-split-receiver-split) is how far he lines up from the
ball or from the formation. You might expect playbooks to give splits in yards ("line up 12 yards from the
ball"), and some do for inside players. For wide receivers, most coaches use **landmarks painted on the field**
instead, because the field isn't symmetric. When the ball is on a hash, a split measured in yards from the
ball would put a receiver near the sideline on one side and nowhere near it on the other.

The main landmark is [**the numbers**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-the-numbers-alignment-landmark): the
big painted yard-line numbers. On an NFL field they start 12 yards in from each sideline and are two yards
tall, so their tops sit about 14 yards from the sideline.[^fieldnums] Receivers align "on the numbers,"
"outside the numbers" (closer to the sideline) or "inside the numbers" (closer to the ball), and the numbers
are in the same place on every snap, whatever the hash.

Inside receivers use different references. A slot receiver typically "splits the difference" between the end
of the line and the outside receiver, and when the ball is on a hash, the other painted landmark, the far
**hash mark**, is a common reference for the slot on the wide side. And outside receivers into the short side usually have a minimum split, a rule such as "never
closer than about six yards to the sideline" or "top of the numbers", so they keep room for a route toward the
sideline. Coaches call a split wider than the landmark a *plus* split and a tighter one a *minus* split. The
details vary by team; the habit of aligning to paint, not to yardage, doesn't.

```{python}
#| label: fig-split-ladder
#| fig-cap: "The split ladder, drawn across the whole field with the ball on the left hash (so the field side is on the offense's right). Four places the right-side receiver (Z) might stand: wide, outside the numbers; on the numbers (the usual landmark, ringed); reduced, inside the numbers; and tight, close to the formation. The grey lanes are the painted numbers, 12 to 14 yards in from each sideline. Because the ball is on a hash, 'on the numbers' is about 17 yards from the ball on the field side but only about 11 on the boundary side, where X stands."
RIGHT_SL, LEFT_SL = HASH_FAR, -HASH_NEAR       # ball on the offense's left hash
LADDER = [("wide", RIGHT_SL - 6.5, "WIDE: outside\nthe numbers", 3.0),
          ("numbers", RIGHT_SL - 13.0, "ON THE\nNUMBERS", 3.0),
          ("reduced", 10.4, "REDUCED: inside\nthe numbers", 5.9),
          ("tight", 6.0, "TIGHT: near\nthe formation", 3.0)]
p = Play(line5() + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, LEFT_SL + 13.0, "X")], None, los=40,
         ball_y="left", to_go=None)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.4))
fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral="full", window=(-8.0, 9.6), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(ax)
numbers_band(fld, p, RIGHT_SL)
numbers_band(fld, p, LEFT_SL)
ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
for key, w, txt, td in LADDER:
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(OFF_D, w))
    draw_marker(ax, float(x), float(y), "off", "Z", ppy, ring=ELIG if key == "numbers" else None)
    leader(fld, p, (td - 0.6, w), (OFF_D + 0.8, w), lw=0.5)
    say(fld, p, td, w, txt, fs=6.3)
hdim(fld, p, -3.9, 0.0, RIGHT_SL - 13.0, "~17 yards from the ball")
hdim(fld, p, -3.9, 0.0, LEFT_SL + 13.0, "~11 yards")
for w in (RIGHT_SL - 13.0, LEFT_SL + 13.0):
    say(fld, p, -6.3, w, "the numbers", fs=6.3, italic=True, box=False, color=style.INK_2)
say(fld, p, 7.8, 23.4, "FIELD SIDE (wide)", fs=6.8, weight="bold", color=style.INK_2)
say(fld, p, 7.8, -13.0, "BOUNDARY (short)", fs=6.8, weight="bold", color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

From the outside in, the ladder looks like this:

- **Wide (outside the numbers).** The receiver is close to the sideline, far from everyone else, with lots of
  room inside him and very little outside. A cornerback can use the sideline as an extra defender. Wide splits
  are common on routes that break *inside*, toward the middle of the field (slants and the like, built in [Part
  4](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)), and on plays where the offense simply wants that
  cornerback as far from the ball as possible.
- **On the numbers.** The default. It leaves room to break either way, and it's far enough out that the
  cornerback has to commit to covering him.
- [**Reduced split**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-reduced-split) **(inside the numbers).** The receiver
  is closer to the ball than his normal landmark. That creates room *outside* him, and it puts him closer to
  the defenders near the ball.
- **Tight (near the formation).** Just a few yards outside the end of the line. Tight splits, and formations
  built from them, are a modern favourite, and they get a full section in
  [Spread Formations](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd).

Why would an offense move a receiver off his landmark? Because a split is a trade of space. A receiver who
needs to run toward the sideline (an out, a corner route) needs room outside him, so he reduces his split to
create it. A receiver who is going to block a linebacker or a safety on a run play (a "crack" block,
[taught in the run game](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd)) wants to start close to his
target, so he reduces too. A receiver who will break inside, or who wants to be one-on-one with a cornerback
and no safety close enough to help, widens out.

That's why splits are tells, the kind you started collecting in [How to Watch a
Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd). **A reduced split often means an
outside-breaking route or a block on the inside; a very wide split often means an inside route or a
one-on-one shot at the cornerback.** Defensive backs are coached to read splits for exactly this reason. And offenses know they are
being read, so good ones vary splits on purpose, using the same reduced split for a crack block one play and a
corner route the next. As with every tell in this book, a split shifts the odds; it never settles them.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"A split is a distance from the ball."** Look at the ladder again. "On the numbers" is about 17 yards from
the ball on the field side and about 11 on the boundary side. The receiver's alignment rule didn't change; the
ball did. This is why a boundary receiver often looks "tight" to a viewer when he is, by his own landmark,
standing exactly where he always stands. Judge a split by the landmarks, not by the gap to the ball.
:::

## Reporting eligible: when a lineman becomes a receiver

Every rule so far has been about *where* players stand. The last one is about *who* they are, and it's the
rule behind the trick plays you'll remember.

Offensive linemen wear numbers from 50 to 79, and in [The Twenty-Two](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd)
you saw why: the number tells the officials, at a glance, that the player is ineligible. But the rules give
the offense a way to change that for one play. [**Reporting
eligible**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-reporting-eligible) works like this:[^reporting]

1. Before the snap, the player wearing an ineligible number goes to the **referee** and tells him he is
   reporting as eligible.
2. The referee tells the defense. The rule only says he "will inform the defensive team"; in practice he
   turns to the defense and announces it, and in the NFL he often also says it over his wireless microphone,
   so the stadium and the broadcast hear "Number 70 is reporting as eligible." Until he has done that and
   returned to his position, the ball can't be snapped. On TV, you'll usually hear it; if you don't, the
   giveaway is a number in the 50s, 60s or 70s standing where a tight end would.
3. The player then lines up where an eligible player can: **at the end of the line, or in the backfield.**
   (Reporting doesn't make an interior lineman eligible; alignment still decides that.)

The rule works in the other direction too. A player wearing an eligible number can report as *ineligible*,
for instance when he lines up where a lineman would. That direction will matter in the film room.

When a lineman reports and lines up at the end of the line, he's an [**eligible
tackle**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-eligible-tackle), or a
[**tackle-eligible**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tackle-eligible) (you'll hear both on broadcasts):
usually a backup tackle playing the role of a sixth lineman, as in the [jumbo](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)
grouping from the last chapter.

```{python}
#| label: fig-reporting
#| fig-cap: "Reporting eligible, step by step, in a goal-line jumbo package (six offensive linemen, two tight ends, two backs; the sixth lineman, #70, is ringed in purple; depth stretched as before). 1: before the snap, #70 tells the referee (striped disc) that he is reporting as eligible. 2: the referee announces it to the defense, and #70 lines up at the left end of the line, where a tight end would stand. 3: the play is a run fake to the right; the defensive end over #70 (E) and the weak-side linebacker (W) chase the fake, and #70 releases up the field into the end zone for a short throw. 4: the same picture without a report: #70 is a blocker only, and a pass to him is a foul. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, N = nose tackle, W/M/S = linebackers, CB = cornerback, SS/FS = safeties."
def jumbo_off(at_ref=False):
    off = line5() + [Player("E70", "OL", "off", LINE_D, -TE_W, label="70"),
                     P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("U", "TE", OFF_D, WING_W + 0.3),
                     P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("FB", "FB", -4.6, 0, "F"), P("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
    if at_ref:
        off = [q.moved(d=-9.2, w=2.6) if q.key == "E70" else q for q in off]
    return off


GL = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -6.0, "E"), D("DLT", "DT", 1.0, -2.4, "T"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"),
      D("DRT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.9, "E"),
      D("WILL", "WILL", 3.4, -3.4), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 3.4, 1.0), D("SAM", "SAM", 2.2, 8.0),
      D("LCB", "CB", 2.0, -8.6, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 4.6), D("FS", "FS", 6.0, -1.6)]
REF = (-10.4, 4.6)          # the referee: about ten yards deep, on the quarterback's throwing-arm side
titles = ["1. Report to the referee", "2. The referee tells the defense", "3. The play: a run fake and a pass",
          "Same picture, no report: 70 is ineligible"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 6.9))
for i, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    p = Play(jumbo_off(at_ref=(i == 0)), GL if i else None, los=107.0, to_go=3)
    p.highlight("E70", color=OL_RING if i < 3 else FOUL)
    if i == 2:
        p.highlight("LE", "WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
        p.path("RB", [(1.2, 2.6), (2.4, 4.6)], delay=0.3)
        p.path("FB", [(2.4, 3.4)], delay=0.1)
        p.path("LE", [(-1.6, 3.4)], delay=0.2)
        p.path("WILL", [(-0.2, 3.0)], delay=0.3)
        p.route("E70", [(1.8, 0.5), (4.0, 0.8), (6.0, 0.8)], side=-1, delay=0.5)
        p.dropback(1.5)
        p.pass_to("E70", t=1.9)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-12.5, 12.5), window=(-12.4, 9.3), title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    ax.set_title(titles[i], loc="left", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    if i in (0, 1):
        referee(fld, p, *REF)
        say(fld, p, REF[0] + 0.1, REF[1] + 1.3, "referee", fs=6.4, box=False, color=style.INK_2, italic=True,
            ha="left")
    if i == 0:
        say(fld, p, -7.0, 7.4, "\"70, reporting\nas eligible\"", fs=6.6)
        say(fld, p, 2.2, -6.8, "goal line = the orange line", fs=6.2, color=style.INK_2, italic=True)
    if i == 1:
        say(fld, p, -7.0, 7.4, "announces it\nto the defense", fs=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -3.9, -7.8, "70 lines up at\nthe end of the line", fs=6.6, color=OL_RING)
    if i == 2:
        say(fld, p, 7.3, -8.2, "70 catches\nit here", fs=6.6, color=OL_RING)
        say(fld, p, -9.6, 5.6, "run fake", fs=6.4, box=False, color=style.INK_2, italic=True)
        say(fld, p, 6.2, 5.6, "E and W chase\nthe run fake", fs=6.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
    if i == 3:
        say(fld, p, -4.2, -6.8, "no report: a blocker only;\na pass to him is a foul", fs=6.6, color=FOUL)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.1, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: reporting"}
The numbering system exists so that **the defense can tell who may catch the ball by looking**. That only works
if exceptions are announced. The reporting rule lets an offense use its linemen creatively (a sixth blocker
who can also catch a pass, a tackle who sneaks out on the goal line), and in exchange it makes the offense
tell the referee, and the referee tell the defense, every time. The defense still has to cover the man; it just
can't be ambushed by him.

Notice the bargain this creates. Panels 2 and 4 of the picture above look identical on the field. What changes
is a sentence said to the referee, so a defense that misses the announcement has to treat every jumbo lineman
as a possible receiver, which is exactly the doubt an offense wants.
:::

How often does it happen? The official play-by-play records each time a lineman reports, so we can count the
six-lineman snaps on which the extra man reported eligible:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (six-lineman snaps and reports, 2016-2025)"
#| output: false
SIX_SEASONS = list(range(2016, 2026))
part = nfl().load_participation(SIX_SEASONS).to_pandas()
plays10 = pbp(SIX_SEASONS, columns=["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "play_type", "down",
                                    "posteam", "pass", "desc"])
plays10 = plays10[(plays10.season_type == "REG") & plays10.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])
                  & plays10.down.notna()]
six = plays10.merge(part[["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "offense_personnel"]], left_on=["game_id", "play_id"],
                    right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"])


def n_linemen(s, season):
    """Offensive linemen in a personnel string. 2016-2022 (NGS) lists linemen only when there are six or
    more ('6 OL, ...'); 2023-2025 (FTN) lists every player by roster position ('1 C, 2 G, 3 T, ...')."""
    if not isinstance(s, str):
        return np.nan
    n = sum(int(k) for k, pos in re.findall(r"(\d+)\s+([A-Z]+)", s) if pos in {"OL", "C", "G", "T"})
    return 5 if (n == 0 and season <= 2022) else n


six["ol"] = [n_linemen(s, y) for s, y in zip(six.offense_personnel, six.season)]
six["reported"] = six.desc.str.contains("reported in as eligible", na=False)
jumbo = six[six.ol >= 6]
tab = jumbo.groupby("season").agg(snaps=("ol", "size"), rep=("reported", "sum"))
tab["share"] = tab.rep / tab.snaps
rep_all = plays10[plays10.desc.str.contains("reported in as eligible", na=False)]
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-jumbo-report
#| fig-cap: "Regular-season runs and passes with six or more offensive linemen, by season (nflverse participation data), split by whether the official play description records a lineman reporting eligible. The percentage above each bar is the share with a report. Six-lineman snaps fell, unevenly, from 2016 to 2020 and jumped in 2025; the share with a report roughly doubled over the decade, from about 40% to about 80%. The participation source changes after 2022 (Next Gen Stats through 2022, FTN from 2023), marked by the dotted line."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.0))
x = np.array(tab.index)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.bar(x, tab.rep, color=OL_RING, width=0.68, label="a lineman reported eligible")
ax.bar(x, tab.snaps - tab.rep, bottom=tab.rep, color="#c9c3ea", width=0.68, label="no report")
for xi, s, sh in zip(x, tab.snaps, tab.share):
    ax.text(xi, s + 25, f"{sh * 100:.0f}%", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.axvline(2022.5, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, ls=(0, (1, 2)))
ax.text(2022.45, 1950, "source change\n(NGS → FTN)", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="top")
ax.set_xticks(x, [str(v) for v in x], fontsize=7.5)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.5)
```
