```{python}
ax.set_ylim(0, 2050)
ax.set_ylabel("snaps with six or more\noffensive linemen", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.legend(loc="upper center", fontsize=7.3, ncol=2, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.1))
ax.set_title("Six-lineman snaps by season", fontsize=9.5)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
assert tab.loc[2025, "rep"] > 1.6 * tab.loc[2024, "rep"] and tab.loc[2025, "share"] > 0.75, tab
assert 0.2 < rep_all["pass"].mean() < 0.3, rep_all["pass"].mean()
```

Two things stand out. First, **2025 was a jumbo year**: about 1,770 six-lineman snaps, close to double 2024,
in the same season that offenses went heavier across the board (the personnel shift in
[Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)). Second, the extra lineman now **reports far more often**. The
share didn't climb every year (it dipped in several), but it roughly doubled over the decade, from about two
snaps in five in 2016 to about four in five in 2024 and 2025, a record.[^jumbodata] A lineman who doesn't
report is simply a blocker. One who does is a blocker the defense can't completely ignore, and the offense
keeps the option of throwing to him. Most of the time it doesn't: across the decade, offenses passed on only
about a quarter of the snaps with a reported lineman. The report is mostly a threat, and the play is mostly a
run.

Why did the habit spread, and why isn't it 100%? The data can't say what coaches were thinking, but the
rulebook shows what the report costs and what it buys. It buys a sixth possible receiver for the defense to
worry about. It costs little: a few seconds while the referee announces it, and a commitment. A reported
player has to keep playing an eligible spot, reporting again before every snap, for as long as he stays in the
game, until a stoppage such as a timeout, a foul or the end of a quarter (or a snap on the sideline) lets him
switch back. An offense that wants him back inside as an ordinary lineman on the next snap, with no time to
substitute, may not want that. And the report itself is a
message: a reported lineman says "big formation, probably a run", which, as the Lions film room below shows,
an offense can use as bait.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: why college and high school are stricter"}
College football doesn't let linemen report eligible at all: NCAA rules require at least five players
numbered 50–79 on the line on a normal scrimmage play, and a player wearing one of those numbers is never an
eligible receiver (the rules loosen only in a punt or field-goal formation).[^ncaa] That's why trick plays to
linemen are an NFL thing. High school had its own scare: in 2007 Piedmont High in California built a whole
offense, the "A-11," from a kick-like formation in which every player wore an eligible number, until the
national high-school rules body closed the loophole in February 2009.[^a11] Rules makers in every league guard
the same principle: the defense must be able to tell who can catch the ball.
:::

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New England Patriots vs. Baltimore Ravens, January 10, 2015"}
This was a divisional-round playoff game of the **2014 season**, played in Foxborough in **January 2015**.
Baltimore led 14–0 in the first quarter and 28–14 in the third, and New England came back both times to win
35–31.[^patsgame] The second comeback started with a formation the Ravens had never seen.

On three snaps of a third-quarter drive, the Patriots lined up with only four offensive linemen. To see why
that forced a report, count the line the way the rules do. Seven men on the line means two ends and **five
players between them, and all five must be ineligible**. Normally those five are the linemen wearing 50–79.
With only four linemen on the field, the fifth interior spot had to go to someone wearing an eligible number,
and the rules say a player whose number doesn't match his spot must tell the referee.[^patscount] So on the
first and the last of the three snaps, running back Shane Vereen (#34) **reported as ineligible** and lined up
in the slot, on the line just inside receiver Julian Edelman. Standing there he was covered anyway, so he was
ineligible twice over: by his position and by his announcement. Meanwhile tight end Michael Hoomanawanui (#47)
lined up at left tackle, with the regular left tackle, Nate Solder, moved inside to guard, which put
Hoomanawanui at the end of the line and made *him* an eligible receiver.[^patsform]

```{python}
#| label: fig-patriots
#| fig-cap: "The Patriots' line on the first of the three snaps, as the Boston Globe described it (schematic: splits are illustrative, and the four players in the backfield are left out). Seven on the line: the ends, #47 Hoomanawanui at the left tackle's spot and #11 Edelman on the right, are eligible (aqua). Between them stand five ineligible players: four linemen, including #77 Solder moved in to guard, and #34 Vereen, who wears a running back's number and so had to report ineligible (red ring)."
pats = [Player("47", "TE", "off", LINE_D, -2 * OL_SPLIT, label="47"),
        Player("77", "OL", "off", LINE_D, -OL_SPLIT, label="77"),
        Player("C", "C", "off", LINE_D, 0.0, label="C"),
        Player("G", "OL", "off", LINE_D, OL_SPLIT, label=""),
        Player("T", "OL", "off", LINE_D, 2 * OL_SPLIT, label=""),
        Player("34", "RB", "off", LINE_D, 9.0, label="34"),
        Player("11", "WR", "off", LINE_D, 15.0, label="11")]
p = Play(pats, None, los=40, to_go=None)
p.highlight("47", "11", color=ELIG)
p.highlight("34", color=FOUL)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.5))
fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-9.5, 20.0), window=(-6.6, 5.6), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(ax)
count_line(fld, p, on_line(p))
# bracket the five players between the ends
(xa, ya), (xb, yb) = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(-2.2, -OL_SPLIT - 0.6)), fld.xy(*p.to_abs(-2.2, 9.6))
ax.plot([float(xa), float(xb)], [float(ya), float(yb)], color=FOUL, lw=1.1, zorder=6)
for w_ in (-OL_SPLIT - 0.6, 9.6):
    (xc, yc), (xd, yd) = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(-2.2, w_)), fld.xy(*p.to_abs(-1.75, w_))
    ax.plot([float(xc), float(xd)], [float(yc), float(yd)], color=FOUL, lw=1.1, zorder=6)
say(fld, p, -3.3, 4.0, "the five between the ends must be ineligible", fs=6.6, color=FOUL)
say(fld, p, -3.6, -6.4, "#47, a tight end at\nthe tackle's spot: eligible", fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, -4.8, 15.0, "#11 Edelman:\nthe right end, eligible", fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, 2.6, 9.0, "#34 Vereen: covered,\nand reported ineligible", fs=6.4, color=FOUL)
plt.show()
```


Here is what the Ravens had to process, in the seconds before the snap:

| Player | What his number said | What he told the referee | What he really was |
|---|---|---|---|
| #34, a running back, standing in the slot | eligible | "I'm ineligible" | ineligible: a decoy |
| #47, a tight end, at the tackle's spot | eligible | nothing | eligible: the end of the line |

Defenders did what they're trained to do: they watched the man wearing a back's number in the slot, and
treated the player in a lineman's spot as a lineman. On the drive, Tom Brady hit Hoomanawanui for 16 yards and then,
on a snap the official play-by-play records with "NE 34-Vereen ineligible," for 14 more to the Baltimore 10.
Ravens coach John Harbaugh came onto the field to protest that his defense hadn't been given time to identify
who was eligible, and the Ravens were penalized for unsportsmanlike conduct on the bench, half the distance to
the goal. Two plays later Brady threw a touchdown to Rob Gronkowski.

Was it legal? Yes. The referee announced each report. Afterwards Brady said the Ravens might want to study the
rule book; Harbaugh called it "clearly deception."[^bradyquote] The league sided, in effect, with both: the formation had
been legal, and it was not going to stay legal. For the **2015 season** the NFL added a rule that a player who
reports as ineligible must line up *inside* the formation's core, roughly between the tackles, so an
eligible-numbered player can no longer report ineligible and then split out where receivers stand. Breaking it
is an illegal substitution, five yards.[^rule2015]

**What to notice:** the trick didn't break the eligibility rules; it broke the defense's *shortcut* for reading
them. Numbers are a convenience. The real rule is position plus announcement, and when an offense separates the
two, the defense has to listen to the referee as closely as it watches the field.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Detroit Lions 2022–2024"}
Under offensive coordinator Ben Johnson (2022–2024), the Lions made the eligible tackle an ordinary part of the
offense rather than a once-a-season gimmick (the Dallas two-point story is in
[Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)). Their reported linemen did catch passes. Right tackle Penei Sewell (#58) reported eligible and caught a
9-yard pass against Minnesota on December 11, 2022, in a 34–23 win; backup tackle Dan Skipper (#70) caught a
4-yarder against the Vikings in Week 18 of 2023 and a 9-yard touchdown against Buffalo on December 15, 2024.
From 2016 to 2025, Lions linemen were thrown to nine times, more than any other team's.[^lionsdata]

But the bigger effect was on everyone else. Detroit reported a lineman on 170 runs and passes from 2022 to 2024,
the third most in the league, and passed on about 35% of them, against about 24% for the league as a whole on
the same kind of snap. The throws mostly went to the regular receivers, off play-action: with Skipper reported
eligible on second-and-5 in that Week 18 game against Minnesota (January 7, 2024), Jared Goff hit Amon-Ra St.
Brown for a 70-yard touchdown.

**What to notice:** a reported lineman forces the defense to account for one more possible receiver *and* tells
it to expect a run. The Lions used the second message more than the first. When you hear "reporting as
eligible," don't watch the lineman. Watch the safeties: if they creep toward the line to stop the run, the
pass that matters is going over their heads.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: the strength caller"}
- **Name the strong side before every snap.** Say it out loud: "tight end right." If there's no attached tight
  end, name the passing strength ("three receivers left") and the field side.
- **Then watch the defense set.** Against a base defense, which side did the Sam (usually the linebacker
  standing over the tight end) and the safety who walks down go to? In nickel there may be no Sam: watch which
  side the defensive tackle lines up just outside a guard (the "3-technique", taught in [Defensive Line
  Play](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd)) and which safety walks
  down ([A First Look at Defense](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) shows how to spot the packages). Did the
  front go one way and the coverage the other? Write down which rule this defense seems to use.
- **Count the line on unusual looks.** Seven or more? Who are the two ends? Is a tight end covered? On a goal
  line or jumbo look, listen for "reporting as eligible."
- **Check the quarterback's depth.** Under center or pistol: lean run, and expect a fake if it's a pass.
  Shotgun: lean pass, and note the back's side.
- **Read the outside receivers' splits against the numbers.** A receiver well inside his usual landmark:
  think crack block or an outside-breaking route. One far outside: think inside route or a one-on-one shot.
- **Log it.** Add "strong side," "QB depth" and "notable split" columns to your [prediction
  log](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd). After a half, check how often the defense set its
  front to the tight end, and how often the quarterback's depth called the run or pass.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: count it"}
First-and-10. The offense comes out in 12 personnel (two tight ends, Y and U) and lines up like this:

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-count
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1. Two tight ends: Y next to the right tackle, U just outside the left tackle. X and Z are wide receivers; R is the running back and Q the quarterback, under center. The dashed line marks a yard behind the line (depth stretched, as in the chapter's other plates)."
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
                 P("U", "TE", OFF_D, -4.7), P("X", "WR", OFF_D, -WIDE), P("Z", "WR", OFF_D, WIDE)]
p = Play(off, None, los=40, to_go=None)
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-9.0, 3.8), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
depth_guide(fld, p, -19.0, 19.0)
plt.show()
```

**Is this formation legal? If not, what's the smallest fix, and who is eligible after it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Illegal formation.** Count the line: the five linemen and Y. That's six. U is a wing (behind the dashed line,
so a yard off the line), and X and Z are both a yard back, so five players are in the backfield: U, X, Z, R and
Q. If the ball is snapped, it's a five-yard flag.

**The smallest fix** is one step forward by one player. The usual one is **X stepping up onto the line**, which
gives seven on the line with X as the left end and Y as the right end. Then the eligible receivers are X and Y
(the two ends) and U, Z and R (the backs); the quarterback under center is not. Another legal fix is **U stepping
up** to become an in-line tight end on the left. That also makes seven, but now U is the left end and X, still a
yard back, is a back. A third fix, **Z stepping up**, also makes seven, but then Z covers Y, who becomes
ineligible: legal, and the wrong fix if you want your tight end in the route (panel 3 of the legality figure).

This is the receiver's question from the opening scene. It's why X checks with the official, and why the
rule about who stands on the line, more than any playbook habit, decides where X and Z line up.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: which side is strong?"}
First-and-10 at midfield, ball on the **right** hash. The offense is in 11 personnel from the shotgun:

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-strength
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2. The ball is on the right hash, so the offense's left is the wide side of the field. The tight end (Y) is attached alone on the left; three receivers (H, Z, X) are on the right, X on the line. The back (R) is beside the quarterback (Q) on his left."
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, -TE_W),
                 P("X", "WR", LINE_D, 15.5), P("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 11.0), P("H", "WR", OFF_D, 7.0)]
p = Play(off, None, los=60, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
p.draw(lateral="full", window=(-8.6, 3.8), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
plt.show()
```

**Name the strong side by each of the three rules. Where is a typical NFL defense likely to set its front, and
which way will its coverage lean? Why might the offense have chosen this arrangement?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**By the tight end: left.** Y is attached on the left. **By the receivers: right**, where three of them stand.
**By the field: left**, because the ball is on the right hash, so the wide side is to the offense's left.

**The likely defense:** against 11 personnel it will usually be a nickel defense, and the front (the
defensive line's shade and the linebackers) sets to the tight end, on the left. With the field also on the left,
there's no argument about it. The coverage has to deal with three receivers on the right, and here's the twist:
they're on the *short* side of the field, the boundary. Most defenses lean their coverage toward the three
receivers anyway, often by rotating a safety down toward them or by playing a "trips check", a coverage
adjustment made only against three-receiver sides (those checks are in [Disguise, Rotation and Split-Field
Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)).

**Why the offense likes it:** putting the receivers into the boundary asks the defense which rule it trusts,
receivers or field, and either answer leaves something open. If the coverage follows the receivers into the
boundary, the wide side is left to the tight end, the back and lots of grass, which is a good place to run or
to throw back to Y. If the coverage stays with the field, three receivers face fewer defenders in a tight space.
The formation's job is to make the defense's own definitions disagree.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: read the alignment"}
First-and-10 at your own 45, ball on the left hash, 12 personnel. Read only what you can see before the snap:

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-tells
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3. The ball is on the left hash (the field side is on the offense's right; the grey lanes are the painted numbers). The quarterback is under center with the back about seven yards deep. Y is in-line on the right with U as a wing outside him. X is on the left and Z on the right."
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
                 P("U", "TE", OFF_D, WING_W + 0.4), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -HASH_NEAR + 7.0),
                 P("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 11.5)]
p = Play(off, None, los=55, ball_y="left", to_go=None)
fld = p.draw(lateral="full", window=(-8.6, 3.8), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
numbers_band(fld, p, HASH_FAR)
numbers_band(fld, p, -HASH_NEAR)
plt.show()
```

**Run or pass? If it's a run, which way? If it's a pass, what kind? What is Z's split telling you?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Lean run, to the right.** Three clues point the same way.

- **The quarterback is under center**, with the back straight behind him. In neutral situations from 2023 to
  2025, offenses passed on only about a third of under-center plays.
- **The strength is right by every rule.** Both tight ends are on the right (Y in-line, U on the wing), and the
  ball is on the left hash, so the right is also the field side, with the most room.
- **Z is in a reduced split**, well inside the numbers on the wide side, where a normal split would put him
  near the numbers about 17 yards from the ball. A receiver that close to the formation is often there to
  block: to crack down on a linebacker or a safety on a run to his side.

**If it's a pass, expect play-action.** About four in five under-center dropbacks used a run fake. The classic
partner of this look is the **bootleg**: fake the run to the right, and the quarterback rolls out to the *left*,
away from the fake, with the reduced Z running a long crossing route back toward him and X, alone wide on the
left, running a comeback or a post behind it. Both receivers' splits make that possible: Z starts close
enough to cross the field in time, and X's wide split leaves room in front of him. ([Play-Action, Boots and
Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) builds the play.)

That's the honest answer to every alignment drill: the picture doesn't tell you the play, it tells you the
*odds*. Here the odds say run right, and if they're wrong, the play-action pass was built to punish exactly the
defense that believed them.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Seven on the line, and the ends are the only eligible linemen.** "On the line" means level with the
  center; "off" means at least a yard back; anything in between is illegal. A player on the line who isn't at
  an end is covered and ineligible.
- **The rules make the letters.** X stands on the line so the formation has an end on his side; Z stands off it
  so the tight end stays eligible and Z can motion. Y is the main tight end; H and F are move players whose
  meaning changes by team and grouping.
- **Strength is a definition, and there are three.** The tight end's side (for the run and the front), the side
  with more receivers (for coverage), and the wide side of the field (the tiebreaker). Offenses win by making
  the definitions disagree.
- **The quarterback's depth is a strong clue.** In 2023–2025 neutral situations, about 69% of shotgun plays were
  passes against about 34% from under center, and about 81% of under-center dropbacks were play-action.
- **Splits are set by landmarks, not yards.** The numbers stay put while the ball moves hash to hash. A reduced
  split often means a crack block or an outside-breaking route; a wide split, an inside route or isolation.
- **A lineman becomes a receiver only by reporting.** The referee tells the defense. The Patriots' January 2015
  trick exploited the defense's reliance on numbers, and since 2015 a player reporting ineligible must line up
  inside the tackles. In 2025 six-lineman snaps nearly doubled, and the extra man reported on about 80% of them.

[^formrules]: NFL, *Official Playing Rules*, Rule 7, Section 5, Article 1 (the offense "must have seven or more players on the line"; eligible receivers on both ends; "No player may take a position that is neither clearly on, nor clearly off the line of scrimmage, unless he is directly behind the snapper"; illegal formation, loss of five yards); Rule 3, Section 18, Article 3 (an offensive player on the line must have his shoulders facing the defense's goal line, and a non-snapper's "helmet must break a vertical plane that passes through the beltline of the snapper"); Rule 8, Section 1, Article 5 (backs are eligible if "legally at least one yard behind the line at the snap"); Rule 3, Section 42 (a T-formation quarterback is "aligned one yard or less behind the snapper"): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^wing]: Referee John Hussey, pool report after the Giants–Commanders game, Dec. 18, 2022, asked whether officials must confirm a receiver's alignment when he checks: "Not typically, and the official could be doing other things, like counting the offense." CBS Sports, Dec. 19, 2022: https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/giants-commanders-official-explains-why-terry-mclaurin-was-flagged-for-illegal-formation-on-critical-play

[^defalign]: NFL, *Official Playing Rules* (2026 edition), Rule 3, Section 18, Article 2 (the neutral zone is "the space between the forward and backward points of the ball") and Section 19 (a player is offside when "any part of his body" is in the neutral zone at the snap); Rule 7, Section 5 sets formation requirements for the offensive team only on a scrimmage down (kickoffs have their own alignment rules): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ . See also "Formation (American football)," Wikipedia ("The defense may line up anywhere on its side of the neutral zone, and players are free to move at any time before the snap"): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formation_(American_football)

[^downfield]: NFL, *Official Playing Rules* (2026 edition), Rule 8, Section 3, Article 1: on a scrimmage play with a legal forward pass, it is a foul "if the entire body of an ineligible offensive player, including a T-Formation Quarterback, is more than one yard beyond the line of scrimmage before the pass has been thrown" (with exceptions for a player who is blocking): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^strengthcalls]: "Rip" and "Liz" as Saban's words for right and left, with "Roscoe and Louie" or a number used by other teams: "When Nick Saban says 'aight', things are not 'aight'," *Tomahawk Nation*, May 21, 2020: https://www.tomahawknation.com/florida-state-football-fsu-noles/2020/5/21/21265925/fsu-nick-saban-rip-liz-pattern-matching-cover-adam-fuller-florida-state-seminoles-football-norvell ; Rip/Liz as a match-coverage family "widely attributed to Nick Saban": FootballScoop, "Rip / Liz match and coverage variations from Indiana Wesleyan defensive coordinator JJ Clark": https://footballscoop.com/rip-liz-match-and-coverages-variations-from-indiana-wesleyan-naia-defensive-coordinator-jj-clark . "Rita Sky!" (strength right, a safety rolling down, Cover 3) and the choice between tight-end and passing strength: Raj Dhami, *The Call Sheet*, June 3, 2024: https://the-call-sheet.beehiiv.com/p/004

[^phillyspecial]: "Philly Special," Wikipedia (Super Bowl LII, February 4, 2018: fourth-and-goal, the ball "snapped to running back Corey Clement," Trey Burton threw to Nick Foles, who had moved up "behind right tackle Lane Johnson"): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philly_Special

[^pistolteams]: Course calculation from FTN charting via nflverse (`qb_location == "P"`), regular-season runs and passes, all situations, 2023–2025 (asserted in the chapter's code): pistol on about 6% of all plays; Atlanta 34.7% of its plays (2024) and 33.1% (2025), Miami 29.1% (2024); Baltimore 7.0% across the three seasons, ninth of 32 teams.

[^patscount]: NFL, *Official Playing Rules* (2026 edition), Rule 7, Section 5, Article 1(b) ("Eligible receivers must be on both ends of the line, and all of the players on the line between them must be ineligible receivers") and Rule 5, Section 3, Article 1 (a player wearing an eligible number "is permitted to line up in the position of an ineligible pass receiver" and "must immediately report the change in his eligibility status to the Referee"); Rule 5, Section 1, Article 2 (eligible receivers wear 0–49 or 80–89): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ . [^reporting]: NFL, *Official Playing Rules*, Rule 5, Section 1, Article 2 (numbering by position: offensive linemen 50–79; eligible receivers wear 0–49 or 80–89, and "all other numerals are worn by ineligible players unless they report a change in their position") and Rule 5, Section 3, Articles 1–2 (the player "must immediately report the change in his eligibility status to the Referee, who will inform the defensive team"; he must stay in that status as long as he is continuously in the game and report again before each play, until a timeout, the end of a quarter, the two-minute warning, a foul, a replay review, a touchdown, a kick, a change of possession, or one snap out of the game): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^jumbodata]: Course calculation from nflverse participation data (`offense_personnel`; six or more players listed as OL, or C + G + T from 2023) joined to nflverse play-by-play, regular-season runs and passes, 2016–2025. "Reported" means the official play description contains "reported in as eligible"; about 98% of those plays are six-lineman snaps. Six-lineman snaps: 1,842 (2016), 841 (2020), 962 (2024), 1,771 (2025). Share with a report: 39% (2016), 80% (2024), 82% (2025). Offenses passed on 21–28% of plays with a report in every season. The description records the referee's announcement; it is not a separate charting field.

The Globe article, Jan. 12, 2015: https://www.bostonglobe.com/sports/2015/01/12/patriots-receiver-eligibility-tactic-could-catch/eTiRiTUbQaECsPGF4e8APJ/story.html , and CBS Sports: https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/harbaugh-says-ne-ran-illegal-plays-tom-brady-says-study-the-rule-book . [^bradyquote]: Brady: "Maybe those guys gotta study the rule book and figure it out." "Harbaugh Says Belichick's Formations 'Clearly Deception'; Brady Says 'Figure It Out'," CBS Boston, Jan. 10, 2015: https://www.cbsnews.com/boston/news/harbaugh-says-belichicks-formations-clearly-deception-brady-says-figure-it-out/

[^rule2015]: Adopted at the league's annual meeting in March 2015 (ESPN, "Patriots' formation now ruled illegal substitution," March 25, 2015: https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/12556985/new-england-patriots-formation-now-ruled-illegal-substitution). The current wording is in Rule 5, Section 3, Article 1: a player with an eligible number who reports ineligible must line up "within the normal five-player core formed by ineligible players and is not more than two players removed from the middle player of a seven-player line"; lining up outside the tackle box is illegal substitution, five yards: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/
